answer:
**In-context learning changes the input context, not the model weights.** You place demonstrations in the prompt, and the model conditions its next-token predictions on them. Fine-tuning instead uses gradients to change parameters. Both can alter behavior, but their storage, cost, and failure modes differ. [1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165)

For example, show `review: wonderful service → positive` and `review: never arrived → negative`, then ask for the label of a new review. The demonstrations communicate the task, output vocabulary, and formatting convention. They can help even when the model already understands the words.

Formally, the prediction is $p_\theta(y\mid D,x)$, where $D$ is the demonstration set. During ordinary inference, $\theta$ stays fixed. A different set or order of examples changes the conditioning sequence and can therefore change the result. This is why “the model learned my examples” should not be interpreted as “the checkpoint was updated.”

Choose demonstrations that represent the actual decision boundaries and output format. Include contrasting cases rather than five nearly identical easy positives. If selecting examples by similarity, avoid leaking the evaluation answer or selecting a near-duplicate of the test item. Keep the instruction and label meanings unambiguous, and measure the effect of example order rather than assuming it is irrelevant.

The practical cost is context length: demonstrations consume tokens on each request and leave less room for the new input. A compact fine-tuned model may be cheaper at large request volume, while prompting can be easier to revise when the task changes. [2](https://web.stanford.edu/~jurafsky/slp3/8.pdf)[3](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)

**Boundary condition:** demonstrations do not guarantee reliable rule induction. A model may exploit superficial patterns, ignore an example, or repeat its mistakes. Evaluate on held-out cases with changed wording and edge conditions. Compare zero-shot, few-shot, and fine-tuned baselines under the same evaluation rather than treating more examples as an automatic improvement.
